title: 道德經 第六章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 6, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 55. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 6 of the Daodejing (成象). The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t:
谷神不死，
是謂玄牝。
玄牝之門，
是謂天地根。
緜緜若存，
用之不勤。

morph.gloss: valley — the hollow between the hills
this — a demonstrative, not yet the modern 'is'
dark — the blue-black of deep water
the female — a dam, the female of an animal
heaven and earth — the cosmos taken as one pair
on and on, unbroken — a doubled word, like thread drawn out without a break
silk floss; a drawn-out thread (usually written 綿 today)
it — here the OBJECT PRONOUN, not the genitive 'of'
to toil, to wear oneself out; here: to be worn out, exhausted

sentences.l:
The valley spirit does not die —
this is called the dark female.
The gate of the dark female —
this is called the root of heaven-and-earth.
Unbroken, unbroken, as if it were there;
use it, and it is never worn out.
sentences.i: The spirit of the valley does not die; it is called the dark female. The gateway of the dark female is called the root of heaven and earth. Drawn out fine and unbroken, it barely seems to be there — yet no amount of use wears it out.
sentences.n: 是謂 is 'this is-called'. 是 here is the demonstrative 'this'; it had not yet become the modern copula, and there is still no verb 'to be' anywhere in this chapter. 谷神 is disputed. Wang Bi takes 谷 as the valley itself — the empty middle that holds nothing and so can hold anything; Heshanggong instead reads 谷 as 養 'to nourish', giving 'he who feeds his spirit does not die', a recipe for long life rather than a cosmology. We follow Wang Bi. 牝 is the female of an animal, a dam — the bearing, receiving side of things; with 玄 before it the phrase names what gives birth without ever being seen. 用之: 之 is the object pronoun 'it' again, not the genitive it was two lines earlier — one character, two jobs, told apart only by where it stands. 勤 ordinarily means 'to toil'; Wang Bi glosses this line with 不勞 'without wearing itself out', which is how we take it. The Mawangdui manuscripts write 堇 in this slot — a phonetic loan for the same word, not a different word, so it settles nothing about the sense. 門, 根, 存 and 勤 all belong to one Old Chinese rhyme group, so four line-ends here chimed together; in Mandarin (mén, gēn, cún, qín) only the first two still do. Worth knowing: the Liezi quotes this whole passage as a saying from the Book of the Yellow Emperor, so it may be older material the Daodejing takes up rather than composes.
